NATIONALS.

I WANTED IT SO BADLY, I FORGOT HOW TO RACE

USA TRIATHLON PARATRIATHLON NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIPS

MILWAUKEE, WI · AUGUST 9, 2026

FINAL PLACING

4TH

FIRST TIME OFF THE PODIUM THIS SEASON

A NOTE FROM PATRICK

It has taken me a few days to admit that to myself and write this email.

USAT Paratriathlon Nationals was the race I had been building toward all year. The goal was the podium. I had worked for it, sacrificed for it, and thought about it for months.

I finished fourth. For the first time this season, I missed the podium.

And honestly, it fucking hurt.

WHAT I COULD HAVE DONE DIFFERENTLY

Not because fourth place is a bad result. It isn’t. But because I knew I was capable of more, and because when I looked honestly at the race, I knew there were things I could have done differently.

I didn’t train enough in the water. I knew swimming was my weakness. I knew it needed more attention, but I thought I could will myself through it and make up the difference on the bike and run.

I couldn’t.

The swim was terrible, and my race was in trouble long before I ever got out of the water. Then I struggled with my prosthetic during pre-transition at the water exit. I fell running with my bike out of T1. Instead of settling down and getting back into my race, I got angry. I rode the bike too hard trying to make up time, burned the match I needed for the run, and eventually blew up.

THE BIGGEST MISTAKE

But the physical mistakes weren’t the biggest lesson I took away from Milwaukee.

The biggest mistake happened in my head.

Not because I didn’t work hard enough. Not because I didn’t want it badly enough. Almost the opposite.

I wanted it so badly that I let the pressure of the goal speak louder than the work I had already done.

I let the other guys unknowingly get in my head. I spent too much of the weekend thinking about who else was racing, how fast they were, what they had done, and what I needed to do to beat them.

I let one bad swim become a bad race. I let anger dictate how I rode the bike. I stopped experiencing the race and started trying to negotiate with it.

I forgot how to race.

THE SWIM · AUGUST 9, 2026

SUNDAY

And that’s a much harder lesson to swallow than finishing fourth.

That realization didn’t happen on Sunday.

Sunday was hard.

I was disappointed. Angry. Bitter. I felt like I had failed. I felt like I had let myself down, and let down my friends, my family, my sponsors, and everyone who had invested in this journey with me.

Then I watched the awards ceremony.

Three other athletes got to experience the moment they had worked their asses off for while I watched from the side stage.

I was genuinely happy for them. I am. But watching someone else live the moment you wanted for yourself is a pretty uncomfortable experience.

Back at the hotel, I told Melissa, “This feeling fucking sucks, and I’m going to make sure I never have to feel this again.” I also told her I was going to use it.

But I needed a few days.

I needed to sit with the emotions instead of immediately trying to turn them into motivation. I went through all five stages of grief, and some of them more than once. I had to reflect honestly: the good, the bad, the mistakes, the progress, and everything in between.

WEDNESDAY

Then on Wednesday, my sister Kayla said something that completely reframed the whole experience for me.

“

Sometimes ‘be harder’ might mean be kinder to yourself. I can’t think of anything harder than that, honestly.

KAYLA · PATRICK’S SISTER

Fuck.

She was right.

In my professional life, I encourage failure. I tell people that failure is where we learn, where we grow, and where we figure out what needs to change. I believe that deeply. But when it was my failure, I struggled to take my own advice.

Maybe that’s part of the lesson.

The question isn’t whether I was good enough. It’s whether I’m brave enough to keep going and find out how good I can be.

SEVEN

Because this is only my seventh race.

Seven. That’s a lot, and it’s also not many. The guys who beat me have years in this sport, training, racing, learning, failing, and figuring things out.

I have one year.

Most people never even start.

But I started.

7

RACES

1

YEAR IN THE SPORT

THE WEEKEND AROUND ME

I’m also not going to let my disappointment take away from what was an incredible weekend for the athletes and community around me.

I’m proud of my teammates and of every athlete who showed up and put themselves on the line in Milwaukee. Congratulations to everyone who raced, podium or not. It takes something to put yourself out there and find out what happens.

And congratulations to the entire Dare2Tri community.

DARE2TRI AT NATIONALS

32

PODIUMS

4

NATIONAL TITLES

That’s fucking incredible.

Being part of this community is one of the things I’m most grateful for. I get to train, race, learn, and grow alongside people who remind me that this sport is about so much more than results.

NOBODY GETS OUT ALONE

BOTH THINGS AT ONCE

So I’m trying to hold both things at the same time.

I can be disappointed in my race and proud of the work that got me there.

And I can be harder on myself without being cruel to myself.

That’s the balance I’m still learning.

So I’m going to keep showing up. I’m going to train the weaknesses instead of trying to will my way through them. I’m going to keep learning how to race instead of only learning how to train. And I’m going to get better at being present enough to enjoy the process.

Because the process is the journey.

And I’m not ready for the journey to end.

Which brings me to what’s next.

WHAT’S NEXT

ONE MORE

SUPERTRI CHICAGO

CHICAGO, IL · AUGUST 23, 2026

My hometown. My home race. One more sprint to close out the season.

This one is going to be different. I’m not interested in spending race week worrying about who is next to me or what someone else is doing. I’m going to race my race, take in the experience, and enjoy the fact that I get to do this at all.

And if you’re in Chicago, come out and make some noise.

Come cheer.

Come heckle.

Come find me on the course and give me a high five.

Come remind me to enjoy the damn thing.

Come have an NA beer afterwards.

I’ve got one more sprint triathlon this season. And I still have a lot to learn.

THANK YOU

To my family, friends, teammates, mentors, sponsors, and everyone who has supported me this year, thank you. Thank you for believing in me, especially when I didn’t have the perspective to believe in myself.

And to the sponsors and partners who make this possible, your support means more than a logo on a race kit. It allows me to chase something that, a year ago, I wasn’t sure was possible.
